purpose: Verify Aircraft Recovery with a compatible spare aircraft: keep downstream flights on time by reassigning F102/F103 to WB4_AC2 while delayed WB4_AC1 rejoins at B and later returns to A on F104.

comparison_logic.explanation: Without using the spare, WB4_AC1 can recover with F101 +60, F102 +30, F103 +20, F104 original, for 110 schedule cost. The spare-aircraft solution keeps F102/F103 on time, so only the forced 60-minute F101 delay remains. Canonical aircraft reassignment cost is zero.

manual_checks: Visualization shows WB4_F101 as the direct disruption exposure.
Recovered F101 uses WB4_AC1 at +60 minutes.
Recovered F102 and F103 remain on original schedule but are assigned to spare WB4_AC2.
WB4_AC2 starts and ends at B with path B-C-B; no ferry is needed.
WB4_AC1 starts and ends at A with recovered path A-B then B-A.
Crew assignments remain WB4_C1 / WB4_C2 / WB4_C2 / WB4_C3 with no crew reassignment or deadhead.
Recovery shows one DELAY action and two AIRCRAFT_REASSIGNMENT actions.
design_notes: A spare-aircraft substitution is used instead of a symmetric tail swap because current aircraft strings enforce required terminal stations. This isolates Aircraft Recovery without adding ferry or terminal-rebalancing complexity.
Both aircraft have equipment type E1, so the spare is equipment-compatible with F102/F103.
The E1 test profile has zero minimum turn time; the spare still has a clear 10-minute ground gap between F102 arrival 10:30 and F103 departure 10:40.
The aircraft reassignment coefficient in phase2_test_v1 is 0, so the swap plan is strictly cheaper than propagating F101 delay through F102/F103.
